sources.excerpt: anch DATE: August 1, 2002 TITLE: VIDEO SURVEILLANCE IN PUBLIC AREAS Directive Statement: The City of Edmonton recognizes the need to balance an individual’s right to protection of privacy against the city’s duty to promote a safe environment for all citizens, and to protect city property. This directive is intended to assist departments in deciding whether collection of personal information by means of a surveillance camera is both lawful and justifiable, and if so, in understanding how privacy protection measures can be built into the use of a surveillance system. It is recognized that each department has unique needs and practices. While these requirements will remain, it is necessary to standardize city procedures in order that all citizens have an expectation of consistency, regardless where the equipment is installed. The purpose of this policy is to: Develop a surveillance system policy that complies with the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act. Ensure consistency of corporate surveillance measures. These guidelines do not apply to covert or overt surveillance cameras being used as a case-specific investigation tool for law enforcement purposes or in contemplation of litigation. They are also not intended to apply to workplace surveillance systems installed to conduct surveillance of employees. sources.excerpt: Township bolstering security at municipal facilities | Corporation of the Township of Esquimalt Skip to main content Township bolstering security at municipal facilities February 3, 2020 Type(s) News Visitors to Esquimalt facilities may observe the addition of cameras in some public spaces in the next week. The cameras will be there to add an additional layer of safety and security for Township staff, clients, visitors, facilities and properties. The Township will be following the rules set out in the Freedom of Information and Personal Privacy Act (FIPPA) and will balance the need to protect municipal assets with individuals’ want of privacy. Signage will indicate where the cameras are located. Records are retained for public safety or security, criminal investigations, evidentiary purposes, as otherwise required by law, or disclosed to a request for access to records under FIPPA; however the Township does not retain the original or a copy of any record for longer than 30 days unless it is flagged for a longer retention. Any records that are accessed or disclosed under FIPPA shall be securely retained by the Township for the required period in accordance with the Township’s Records Management Policy. Any questions about the collection of personal information or requests for access to records may be directed to the Corporate Officer, Township of Esquimalt, 1229 Esquimalt Road, Esquimalt, BC V9A 3P1, or by telephone at 250-414-7135. More information about privacy and video recording can be found at Esquimalt.ca/privacy . Category Esquimalt News

Numerous evaluations have been conducted by the Fire Service using decades of data and the results are consistent. Working smoke alarms save lives. Statistics show that smoke alarms help save lives, reduce fire related injuries, reduce the spread of fires, and reduce the damage caused by fire. International studies show that your chances of dying in a home fire may be reduced by 5o percent if a working smoke alarm is present in your home. Most fire deaths happen in homes as a result of people breathing smoke and toxic fumes while they are asleep. Smoke alarms are an effective early warning device that can awaken sleeping occupants and help provide time to safely exit the building. Smoke alarms are mandatory in all dwellings (homes and sleeping rooms). Under the British Columbia Fire Code all homes, and all sleeping rooms within boarding and lodging houses, hotels and recreational cabins, are required to be protected by smoke alarms. Dwelling units constructed before the British Columbia Building Code required smoke alarms in 1979 are also required to have a smoke alarm. Smoke alarms are permitted to be battery operated in a dwelling unit constructed before the March 31, 1979 British Columbia Building Code inception date or in a building which is not supplied with electrical power. Terms of Service and Agreement Collection Notice The personal information on this form is collected by the City of Prince George for the purposes of facilitating the CCTV Registry Program under the authority of section 26(c) of the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act . If you have any questions about the collection of your personal information, to update or correct your information, or to opt out of the program, please contact the Manager of Police Support Services at 455 Victoria Street, Prince George, B.C., or by telephone at 250-561-3300 or email at cctvregistry@princegeorge.ca . Terms of Service The CCTV Registry allows you to proactively participate in the enhancement of your community’s public safety by confidentially and voluntarily registering your surveillance recording camera(s) with the City of Prince George. By registering your surveillance equipment, you will be helping law enforcement quickly identify the location and owners of potential sources of video evidence, decreasing time, effort, and cost of an incident investigation. By voluntarily registering your camera equipment with the City of Prince George, you acknowledge and agree to the following: You are registering only those cameras that you own and manage. The information you voluntarily register (your contact information and camera location details) will be confidentially managed by the City of Prince George and securely shared with law enforcement for the sole purpose of identifying potential recorded video footage related to a law enforcement investigat
sources.scope: Voluntary owner-managed camera registry; police contact owners for potential evidence.

cctv.heading: Prepare owner-controlled footage retrieval before registry participation
cctv.body: Prince George’s CCTV Registry Program is voluntary and requires participants to register cameras they own and manage. Its terms describe confidential handling of contact and camera-location information so law enforcement can identify potential recorded evidence and contact the owner. For a participating property, verify the accountable contact, camera inventory and a practical method for finding and exporting relevant footage. Keep registry details accurate when ownership or equipment changes, and establish a separate process for reviewing requests. Registration is not permission for unrestricted live police access and does not replace the owner’s privacy assessment. The programme also does not establish that a recording will exist when investigators request it.

sources.excerpt: Video Surveillance Policy – CCR-6 Effective: June 4, 2019 Authorized By: Council Resolution: 19-15-283 Replaces: April 26, 2010, March 27, 2018 Scope The City of Quesnel in its’ commitment to public safety has initiated a program to deter and prevent nuisance, mischief, theft and vandalism in, on or near property and facilities owned or occupied by the City and to support law enforcement, through the use of video surveillance cameras at certain locations of our open public areas. Safeguards will be implemented to protect the privacy of our citizens while at the same time providing enhanced safety in the use and enjoyment of the public space in our community. The program is intended to be consistent with the Privacy Act of Canada and the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act of British Columbia. DEFINITIONS “Acts” mean the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act, RSBC 1996, c. 165 and the Privacy Act of Canada. “FOI Head” means the person or persons designated to act on behalf of the City for the purposes of the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act and to carry out the powers, duties and functions of the head under the Act. “Guidelines” mean the “Guidelines for the Use of Video Surveillance of Public Places by Police and Law Enforcement Authorities” published by the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, or similar guidelines published by the Information and Privacy Commissioner of British Columbia, both as may be amended or replaced from time to time. “Personal Information” means recorded information about an identifiable individual as defined under the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act. “Open Public Space” means the grounds of any real property, or portions of real property, owned or subject to a rig

cctv.heading: Define the civic public-space purpose before extending a view
cctv.body: Quesnel’s Video Surveillance Policy CCR-6 describes cameras at certain open public areas in or near City-owned or occupied property to deter nuisance, mischief, theft and vandalism while protecting privacy. This is a municipal programme with a defined public-space scope, not a rule requiring cameras at every local business. For a civic expansion, map the proposed view against the documented incident and identify unnecessary neighbouring capture before selecting lenses or positions. Assign responsibility for approval, recording access and incident preservation in the project brief. Confirm whether the June 2019 policy has later amendments. Its stated purpose does not prove present camera coverage or justify unrelated analytics.

sources.excerpt: Cybersecurity & Email Safety - City of Richmond, BC Skip to main content Cybersecurity & Email Safety The City of Richmond, like many organizations, can be a target for cybercrime. We have experienced instances of cybercrime over the past few months and continue to work to prevent such attacks and protect the information and online safety of our customers and staff. We are aware that some fraudulent email messages have been circulating claiming to be from City staff, municipal officials, and Gateway Theatre staff. When the City discovered the intrusion into the email system in June 2023, it took immediate steps to mitigate the risk of impact and remediate the attack by engaging a team of cybersecurity experts to contain and investigate the incident, in accordance with industry best practices. There is no indication any outside party has accessed the City’s financial or human resources data, or any other enterprise systems or databases. City operations were not impacted and business continues as normal. However, in the interest of transparency, we want people to know that fraudulent emails continue to circulate. The following provides important information about the City's ongoing cybersecurity initiatives and how to remain safe in an online environment. What has the City of Richmond done? The City of Richmond engaged cybersecurity experts in June 2023 to investigate, contain and remediate the incident that occurred at that time. The City also placed a public warning regarding fraudulent e-mails on its website, and social media channels. Local media was also advised of the situation. sources.title: Video Surveillance Policy
sources.excerpt: POLICY OBJECTIVES: The Video Surveillance Policy aims to: 1. improve and maintain the personal safety of our staff members and citizens by deterring criminal conduct in regards to harassment, assault, thefts or vandalism; 2. assist with the continued integrity, public confidence, security and protection of any or all municipal properties and assets; 3. minimize impacts on personal privacy by reserving the use of any video surveillance technology for legitimate law enforcement purposes; 4. confirm video surveillance equipment is restricted so it cannot be adjusted or manipulated by anyone to overlook spaces that are not intended to be covered by the video surveillance system, 5. ensure applications of video surveillance in City of Rossland facilities and operations are authorized and are compliant with the British Columbia Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act (FOIPPA). POLICY BACKGROUND/SCOPE: Closed Circuit Video Surveillance (CCTV) is used to serve as a deterrent with respect to criminal activity and ensure proper conduct is administered in relation to City staff members, customers and assets. The City recognizes that any video surveillance technology has a high potential for impacting general individual expectations to privacy and does not wish to breech personal privacy any more than is warranted to provide reasonable protection to City related property. However, the City of Rossland also recognizes the need to strike a balance between an individual’s right to be free from invasion of privacy and the City’s duty to promote a safe environment which protects the security of its staff members, citizens, municipal resources and property. DEFINITIONS: There are no specific terms that need to be defined to understand this policy. Video Surveillance Page 1 o

cctv.heading: Prevent camera adjustment from expanding an authorized view
cctv.body: Rossland’s Video Surveillance Policy explicitly seeks to restrict equipment so it cannot be manipulated to overlook spaces not intended for coverage. Its scope concerns City facilities and operations and balances asset protection with personal privacy. A municipal camera design should therefore document the intended scene, mounting constraints and who can change orientation or configuration. Include a check after servicing so a repaired or replaced unit does not silently capture additional space. For a private property this is a scoped governance example, not a binding installation standard. Confirm the applicable current policy and approvals; the policy’s objectives do not establish present camera locations or continuous operator observation.

The Video Monitoring Policy promotes certainty and predictability by creating specific rules around the installation and use of cameras by the City of Vernon, and providing for meaningful oversight of compliance with these rules. The Video Monitoring Policy The Video Monitoring Policy was developed by Senior Managers and reviewed and approved by the Chief Administrative Officer. The policy and the program was implemented due to ongoing public requests to improve safety and security in certain areas of the City. cctv.heading: Voluntary camera registration and evidence handover
cctv.body: Fredericton’s Community Camera Registry is voluntary and does not give police direct access to cameras or live feeds. A useful CCTV plan should therefore separate camera administration from any later decision to share evidence. Record each camera’s location, viewing direction and retention time, since these are the details the registry requests, and keep those records current when equipment changes. Identify who can approve a footage request and who can export a usable clip. Participation can be updated or removed; build that review into ownership changes. The registry is an evidence-location resource, not a substitute for monitoring or a promise of police response.
cctv.independentReviewReason: The full registry source explicitly supports voluntary participation, no direct camera/live-feed access, requested locations/viewing directions/retention times, and updating or withdrawing registration. consulting.heading: Check alteration approvals before finalizing the security design
consulting.body: Bonavista asks permit applicants for supporting documentation including construction plans or a façade sketch and a site or proposal sketch. For a security upgrade, use an early planning consultation to describe the actual work rather than assuming that every device either needs a permit or is exempt. Bring proposed mounting positions, cable routes and any door, wall or exterior changes to the relevant permitting staff. Keep the resulting advice with the project drawings and resolve design changes before work starts. This is a planning application of the published permit guidance, not a claim that the municipality specifically regulates every security installation. Heritage status and the precise scope of alterations should be checked for the individual property.
consulting.independentReviewReason: The opening municipal permit fact is supported, but the source is general construction/development permitting, not a differentiated site security assessment. The remaining security-upgrade, cable-route, drawings and heritage-check language is the same generic template across six cities after differing introductory facts. Scoped planning language avoids a universal permit claim but does not establish target-service relevance; reject permit padding rather than treat it as security-consulting evidence.

intrusion.heading: Reduce nuisance activations before handover
intrusion.body: Halifax’s security and fire alarm guidance makes property owners responsible for keeping alarm equipment working properly and explains its false-alarm process. The technology may or may not record sound or include analytics such as facial recognition. Privacy is a human right and it is important that your security camera is installed and used in a way that considers the privacy of residents and neighbours. The City does not regulate the use of security cameras on private residential properties, but there are best practices you should consider when installing a camera on your property. These guidelines are not for the use of security cameras in public spaces or private spaces owned by commercial, industrial and retail enterprises. Installing Security Cameras Disputes Over Security Cameras Consider the following best practices for the installation and use of security cameras on private residential properties, so that the privacy of residents and neighbours is respected. You can reduce the potential impact to your neighbours and people walking near your home by: Taking efforts to ensure that the camera only records footage of your property. sources.excerpt: Using a Security Camera on Your Property – City of Toronto Skip to content Using a Security Camera on Your Property Property owners and residents may choose to use security cameras on private properties for a number of reasons, such as identifying visitors and ensuring the security of delivered packages. These may include “doorbell” cameras (for example, Google Nest and Ring) and other cameras that can be installed inside or outside homes to record footage outside. The technology may or may not record sound or include analytics such as facial recognition. Privacy is a human right and it is important that your security camera is installed and used in a way that considers the privacy of residents and neighbours. The City does not regulate the use of security cameras on private residential properties, but there are best practices you should consider when installing a camera on your property. These guidelines are not for the use of security cameras in public spaces or private spaces owned by commercial, industrial and retail enterprises.          Un comité d’accès à l’information et à la protection des renseignements personnels, ci-après

      Dans le but d’orienter ses choix de mesures de sécurité de l’information, ce comité :
          •   Procède à l’identification et l’évaluation périodiques des risques qui menacent la
              confidentialité, l’intégrité ou la disponibilité de l’information;
          •   Déploie des mesures de protection en fonction de l’évaluation des impacts et de la

          •   Procède à une évaluation des risques et à une évaluation des facteurs relatifs à la vie

              changement important à ses systèmes d’information ou des infrastructures
              informationnelles. Une ÉFVP est une démarche préventive qui vise à mieux protéger les
              renseignements personnels et à respecter la vie privée des personnes physiques. Elle
              consiste à considérer tous les facteurs qui auraient des conséquences positives et
              négatives sur le respect de la vie privée des personnes concernées.


7.2   Plan de relève et de continuité
      La continuité des activités nécessaires à la réalisation de sa mission est assurée en tout temps,

      essentielles. Un plan des mesures d’urgence, prévoyant notamment une cellule de crise ainsi
      que des mesures d’urgence, est élaboré et maintenu à jour afin de limiter les impacts liés à un
      incident majeur.


7.3   Gestion des accès
      Un contrôle de l’accès aux locaux, de même qu’aux informations de manière à empêcher tout
      accès non autorisé, dommage ou intrusion est fait par la Ville. L’accès à l’information n’est
      permis qu’aux personnes détentrices de celle-ci et aux personnes autorisées par celles-ci,
      incluant les fournisseurs de service.


7.4   Sécurité physique
      Des mesures adéquates pour protéger ses informations et ses systèmes d’information contre
      toute atteinte à leur intégrité, incluant notamment contre les risques d’incendie, d’inondation,
      de survoltage, de coupures de courant et autres pannes de diverses natures, sont prises par la
      Ville.


7.5   Cycles de vie des systèmes d’information
      Les systèmes d’information permettent de protéger la confidentialité et l’intégrité de

      en ce sens et suivies tout au long du processus menant à l’acquisition, au développement, à

7.1   Gestion du risque
         Un comité d’accès à l’information et à la protection des renseignements personnels, ci-après

                                                    7
       protection des renseignements personnels, de même que pour le suivi des incidents de
      confidentialité.
      Dans le but d’orienter ses choix de mesures de sécurité de l’information, ce comité :
          •   Procède à l’identification et l’évaluation périodiques des risques qui menacent la
              confidentialité, l’intégrité ou la disponibilité de l’information;
          •   Déploie des mesures de protection en fonction de l’évaluation des impacts et de la
              probabilité d’occurrence d’une menace, de façon à atténuer les risques et à les
              maintenir à un niveau acceptable;
          •   Procède à une évaluation des risques et à une évaluation des facteurs relatifs à la vie
              privée, ci-après dénommée « ÉFVP » préalablement à toute acquisition ou tout
              changement important à ses systèmes d’information ou des infrastructures
              informationnelles. Une ÉFVP est une démarche préventive qui vise à mieux protéger les
              renseignements personnels et à respecter la vie privée des personnes physiques. Elle
              consiste à considérer tous les facteurs qui auraient des conséquences positives et
              négatives sur le respect de la vie privée des personnes concernées.


7.2   Plan de relève et de continuité
      La continuité des activités nécessaires à la réalisation de sa mission est assurée en tout temps,
      y compris lors d’un sinistre ou d’une défaillance majeure affectant les informations jugées
      essentielles. Un plan des mesures d’urgence, prévoyant notamment une cellule de crise ainsi
      que des mesures d’urgence, est élaboré et maintenu à jour afin de limiter les impacts liés à un
      incident majeur.


7.3   Gestion des accès
      Un contrôle de l’accès aux locaux, de même qu’aux informations de manière à empêcher tout
      accès non autorisé, dommage ou intrusion est fait par la Ville. L’accès à l’information n’est
      permis qu’aux personnes détentrices de celle-ci et aux personnes autorisées par celles-ci,
      incluant les fournisseurs de service.


7.4   Sécurité physique
      Des mesures adéquates pour protéger ses informations et ses systèmes d’information contre
      toute atteinte à leur intégrité, incluant notamment contre les risques d’incendie, d’inondation,
      de survoltage, de coupures de courant et autres pannes de diverses natures, sont prises par la
      Ville.


7.5   Cycles de vie des systèmes d’information
      Les systèmes d’information permettent de protéger la confidentialité et l’intégrité de
      l’information et assurer sa disponibilité. Des mesures d’encadrement et de suivi sont établies
      en ce sens et suivies tout au long du processus menant à l’acquisition, au développement, à
      l’implantation et à l’entretien des systèmes d’information, de même que tout au long de leur

          cycle de vie de l’information, soit pendant l’ensemble des étapes de son traitement que sont la

         Le maintien de différents mécanismes de surveillance afin de détecter les défaillances des
         systèmes d’information, de même que toute utilisation non autorisée ou malveillante est
         assurée par la Ville.


   7.7   Gestion des incidents de confidentialité et de sécurité de l’information
         La Ville élabore et applique des procédures de gestion des incidents de confidentialité et de
         sécurité, de manière à traiter efficacement tout événement qui cause un dommage à une
         information ou un système d’information et prévenir tout acte ou omission qui entraîne ou
         pourrait entraîner la matérialisation d’un risque.
